this Convention in particular:
WHEREAS: Robert Michelet, Zeta '34, died suddenly March 14,
1934 in his senior year on the threshold of a life giving promise of great
brilliancy and usefulness, having achieved unusual honors while an
undergraduate as a student, athlete, a college leader, a member of Phi
Beta Kappa and a Rhodes Scholar Elect and
WHEREAS: The Psi Upsilon Fraternity of which he was a member
and President of the Zeta Chapter shares with the coUege world a feeling
of loss at his premature death now be it
Resolved: That the Psi Upsilon Fraternity in Convention assembled
express to, Dartmouth College and to the Zeta Chapter its deepest sym
pathy in the loss of so splendid a young man on the threshold of his
career and be it further
Resolved: That a copy of this resolution be sent to his family, to
the President of Dartmouth College, and to the Zeta Chapter of the Psi
Upsilon Fraternity.

Appendix A
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
OF THE
EXECUTIVE COUNCIL OF THE PSI UPSILON FRATERNITY
HELD UNDER THE AUSPICES OF THE
EXECUTIVE COUNCIL
APRIL 28, 1934
The Executive Council welcomes the delegates to this, the 1934 Con
vention of Psi Upsilon. This is the second time since the founding of the
Council in 1869 that a Convention has been held under its auspices instead
of as the guests of a particular Chapter �
the previous occasion was in 1918.
After the founding of Psi Upsilon in 1833 the first official Convention
was held in 1840 with the Beta Chapter at Yale University. In previous
years informal meetings were held, attended by representatives of the then
existing Chapters. There is no record of a Convention in 1842 but the Epitome
says "yet it seems probable that one was held". The only other year in
which a Convention was not held was in 1917 which was due to the outbreak
of the Great War.
In view of the extensive celebration in connection with our Centennial
last November, the Executive Council deemed it advisable to hold just a
one day Convention this year in order to transact the necessary business of
the Fraternity and, at the same time, incur as little expense as possible for
the Fraternity nationaUy and the several Chapters individuaUy.
General Fraternity Conditions; In completing this, the fifth college
year since the beginning of the current depression, it is worthy to note, in
passing, the outstanding manner in which the Psi Upsilon has weathered the
storm. It is well to compare our status with that of the other societies in this
regard. Due to the loyalty, devotion and conservative good judgment on the
part of our Chapters who have acted in concert with the kindly interested
supervision of our alumni, we are proud of our record of achievement during
these trying times.
Chapter Reports: Due to our lack of time in this one day Convention
the oral report of each Chapter must necessarily be brief and to the point.
Voting on Petitions: Pursuant to the action of the 1933 Convention
the petitions of the "Wranglers" of Northwestern University and of Alpha
Kappa Alpha of the University of British Columbia were submitted to the
Chapters for ratification vote. The results of this action were as foUows:

The Finances of Psi Upsilon: We wish to recall to the minds of the
delegates and alumni present, that there is no other society to our knowledge
which operates on such a smaU budget as we do in the matter of national
fraternity expenditure. We adhere strictly to the poKcy of paying no salaries
to any member of our society for services rendered. There are other coUege
fraternities which have payrolls of considerable amount including salaries for
such officers as President, Executive Vice-President, Secretary, Treasurer,
Editor of Magazine, TraveUng Secretaries and a corps of office help. Our
sole national expenditure consists of maintaining a very modest office in
charge of one employee. A careful perusal of the report of the Treasurer of
the Council will Ust the other nominal items of expenditure. Insofar as we
are aware, our annual tax of $4.00 per year per undergraduate is the lowest
of any of the societies. Furthermore, we wish to point out that we are practicaUy the only prominent or weU known college society which did not raise
an endowment fund some time between 1920 and 1930. It was believed by
your Executive Council that we had no need for such funds and that aU monies
which our interested alumni might donate to the Fraternity would better be
used in gifts to their own Chapters.
You wiU note from the report of our Treasurer, that about 10% of our
income from annual taxes is expended in rebating up to $150 per year, to
both the Epsilon and the Theta Theta Chapters, on their costs of sending a
delegate to the Annual Convention. This is in accordance with general
resolution No. 3 of the 1924 Convention. Prior to the 193S Convention the
Executive Council wiU disseminate such data as wiU enable that Convention
to take appropriate and equitable action.
Chapter Histories; Little progress can be reported by the Council in
the matter of compilation of Chapter histories since the Convention of last
November. We now have on file the completed histories of the Theta, Delta,
Gamma, and Upsilon. The Zeta and the Xi have reported that their histories
are in the process of preparation. This is an essential obUgation of each
Chapter and we beheve it merits a Convention resolution.
Election to the Executive Council: We call your attention to the
fact that the terms of Emmett Hay Naylor, Zeta '09, and A. Avery HaUock,
Xi '16, expire with this Convention. It is therefore incumbent upon this
Convention to elect two Brothers to serve for the ussual terms of five years
each and in addition, in accordance with the amendment to our Constitution,
passed in 1932, it wiU be necessary for you to elect a third Brother for the
additional membership on the CouncU thus provided for.

The Council wishes to report that Brother Samuel M. Havens, Upsilon
'99, who was elected by the last Convention to fill a vacancy, (caused by the
resignation of Brother Corcoran) found it impossible to accept his election
due to pressure of business and personal matters. We wish to report that, in
accordance with the Constitution, the Council has fiUed this interim vacancy
by persuading Brother Corcoran to fill-out his own term expiring with the
1935 Convention.
Scholarship: Continued progress by our Chapters in giving proper
emphasis to the matter of scholarship is hereby acknowledged. We do ad
vocate the necessity of each Chapter maintaining such supervision over its
scholarship problems as wiU keep Psi Upsilon in its proper relative standing
as compared to its rivals and, what is more important, in impressing our
undergraduates with the necessity of training themselves in a discipUne of the
mind so as to best fit each of our undergraduate members for their business,
professional and social careers. Each Chapter wiU report its own scholarship
achievements including election of many men to the honor scholastic societies
and the election of three of our undergraduates as Rhodes Scholars, one each
from Zeta, Omicron and Nu.
1935 Convention: The Beta Beta Chapter invited the 1934 Convention
to their Chapter at Trinity College, Hartford, Connecticut. They accepted
the suggestion of the Executive Council that this be postponed until 1935
when a regular three-day session can be held. The Beta Beta Chapter desires
an opportunity to be host for the next regular Convention. Their request
was granted tentatively but should be confirmed by this Convention.
Our Alumni: It was to be expected that the demands of the times have
been such as to prevent many of our alumni from participating in the affairs of
their Chapters or the fraternity in general, as actively as they might desire.
These trying times have been a severe test to many of our alumni and we are
proud of the manner in which nearly all of them have "seen the job thru".
We are pleased to note the policies of a number of our Chapters in intensifying
the work of their "Alumni Cultivation Committee". It is essential that we
keep before our alumni our spirit and purposes. We believe in an emphasis on
our splendid heritage of fine friendships among men of similar tastes and
mutual regard. Our Chapters should continue to lay stress on this thought.
Petitions: We have received a petition again this year from the Alpha
Kappa Alpha society from the University of British Columbia for a charter
and submit same for your consideration. We understand that the President
of their Chapter has come from Vancouver to address you and he is accom
panied by one of their alumni who is now in a graduate school in the East.
They respectfully request a hearing.
RespectfuUy submitted,
LeRoy J. Weed, Theta '01, Secretary
Executive Council of Psi Upsilon.

Archibald Douglas, Lambda '94, President

REPORT OF THE TREASURER
1934
There is here presented a statement of the Net Worth as of April 24,
1934, of the various funds of the Fraternity held by the Executive CouncU
and also the Income and Expense Accounts of the funds for the period Novem
ber 1, 1933 to April 24, 1934. Usually the Treasurer's report covers a fuU
year from one convention until the next, but this report covers six months
only, due to the fact that the Centennial Convention was held in November.
A list of the investments held by the various funds is shown on page 17.
It is to be noted that there was a cash deficit of $2,236.42 in the general
Fund, which in effect means that the General Fund has had to borrow cash
from the other funds to meet its cash requirements. This cash deficit wiU be
diminished as other assets of the General Fund such as Receivables, Directo
ries, Song Books and Song Records are converted into cash.
The income and expense accounts of the various funds are self-explana
tory except that some comment might be made concerning the Centennial
Fund. After pajring over |5,000 for the Memorial, making a $1,000 grant to
the Theta Chapter, and defraying certain preliminary expenses, the Net
Worth of the Centennial Fund as of October 31, 1933 was $10,006.05, repre
sented by $2,506.05 of cash and receivables and $7,500.00 book value of
investments. The sale of these investments (1200 Trust Certificates of United
States Electric Light and Power Shares, Inc., Series "B") produced $2,580
cash, involving a loss of $4,920 as shown in the accounts. The cash on hand
November 1, 1933 together with that reaUzed from the sale of the USELPS
Certificates and otherwise was aU spent during the period in defraying Cen
tennial expenses, the largest items of which were (1) a proportion of the
printing biU for the number of the Diamond which carried the Centennial
announcements, (2) program and general printing biUs for the Centennial,
and (3) the balance of the cost of the Centennial Banquet in Schenectady
which was not covered by receipts in Schenectady but was paid by the Exec
utive CouncU m accordance with its resolution passed April 17, 1934. After
meeting all these expenses there was a deficit of $21.20 in the Centeimial Fund,
as shown m the Net Worth statement. This deficit has since been absorbed
by the General Fund.
The Treasurer wishes to point out that every endeavor is being made
to keep expenses, and therefore the Chapter taxes, at a minimum. With the
elimination of the taxes for Centennial purposes, taxes amount to $4 per man
per year, which is low in relation to the taxes of other fraternities.
